What Does a Community Nurse Do? Clinical Care at Home Under the NDIS

The clinical tasks an NDIS community nurse covers at home, and where the role stops.

A community nurse is a registered nurse who delivers clinical care in your home instead of a hospital or clinic. Wound dressings, catheter and bowel care, tube feeding, medication management, health assessments. They also write the plans your support workers follow and train those workers on your specific routine, which is the part most people do not realise until something goes wrong.

That second half of the job is the reason I wanted to write this. Families usually picture a nurse as someone who turns up, does a dressing and leaves. In a complex care arrangement the nurse is closer to the architect. They hold the clinical picture, decide what can safely be delegated to a support worker, and change the plan as the person's needs change. When community nursing care is missing from an arrangement that needs it, the gap does not show up straight away. It shows up at the first hospital readmission.

Here is what the role actually covers, where it stops, and how it is funded.

What a community nurse does on a visit

A visit usually has three parts, and only one of them is the hands-on task.

The first is assessment. Skin integrity, hydration, pain, bowel and bladder function, respiratory status, how the equipment is holding up, how the person seems compared with last fortnight. A nurse is trained to notice deterioration early, and early is where the value sits.

The second is the clinical task itself. Changing a dressing, replacing a catheter, flushing a feeding tube, administering an injection, checking a tracheostomy site.

The third is the part that carries past the visit. Updating the care plan, writing or revising the instructions support workers follow, signing off a worker as competent on a particular task, and liaising with the GP, the specialist, the pharmacist or the support coordinator. A nurse who visits fortnightly may only be in the house for an hour, but the plans they leave behind govern what happens on the other thirteen days.

Community nurse or support worker, where the line sits

The honest answer is that the line moves, and a nurse is the person who decides where it sits for you.

Some clinical tasks can be delegated to a trained support worker once a nurse has assessed the person, written the procedure and signed the worker off as competent on it. Others cannot be delegated at all and must be done by a registered nurse every time. Which is which depends on the task, the person's stability and the nurse's clinical judgement, not on what is convenient for the roster.

This is also where high intensity daily personal activities and community nursing meet. Those eight supports are delivered by support workers, but the NDIS Practice Standards expect a suitably qualified health practitioner behind them. In practice that is usually the nurse.

The clinical tasks that need a nurse

The common ones in disability support are these.

  • Wound and pressure care. Assessing, dressing and reviewing pressure injuries, surgical wounds and chronic ulcers, and escalating when healing stalls.
  • Continence and catheter management. Indwelling and suprapubic catheter changes, bladder washouts, continence assessment and planning.
  • Bowel care. Establishing and reviewing a bowel programme, which is particularly common after spinal cord injury.
  • Enteral feeding. Tube site care, troubleshooting blockages, reviewing the regimen with a dietitian, retraining workers when the setup changes.
  • Respiratory support. Tracheostomy site care and suctioning, oxygen management, oversight of ventilator routines.
  • Medication management. Webster pack reviews, injections, PRN protocols, and checking that what is in the house matches what the GP last prescribed.
  • Diabetes and chronic condition monitoring. Blood glucose patterns, foot checks, escalation thresholds.
  • Seizure and epilepsy management plans. Written protocols covering what workers do, when, and at what point an ambulance is called.

For someone living with a spinal cord injury, several of these run at once and interact with one another, which is exactly why they need a single clinician holding the whole picture rather than separate services each managing their own piece.

How it is funded in an NDIS plan

Community nursing is funded when the clinical need is disability related. That distinction is where most of the confusion lives.

If you need wound care because of a pressure injury caused by immobility from your disability, that sits with the NDIS. If you need wound care after an unrelated operation, that is the health system. Plenty of real situations sit in the middle, and a nursing assessment is often what settles the argument either way.

The funding usually appears in Core Supports as a nursing or high intensity line, or in Capacity Building where the work is assessment and plan development rather than ongoing care. The NDIA publishes current price limits in its Pricing Arrangements and Price Limits, updated each financial year, so your plan manager or support coordinator is the right person to confirm today's rate.

One practical point. Nursing hours are often underfunded in plans simply because nobody asked for them. If a nurse has assessed you and written a recommendation, that document is evidence for a plan reassessment. Without it the NDIA has nothing to act on.

When a nurse should be involved and often is not

Some moments reliably call for nursing input, and they are the moments it is most often skipped.

  • Coming home from hospital. The ward has been managing a wound, a tube or an airway. On discharge that responsibility transfers to a household, and somebody has to translate the hospital plan into instructions a support worker can follow. Teams that work with hospital discharge planners will usually ask for a nursing assessment before the discharge date is fixed rather than after.
  • After any change in equipment or medication. A new tube, a different dressing product, a changed dose. The old worker instructions are now out of date, and nobody will notice until there is a problem.
  • When a condition is progressing. Needs that were stable six months ago may not be stable now. A periodic review catches the drift.
  • When the same problem keeps recurring. Repeated urinary tract infections, a wound that will not close, recurring chest infections. A pattern like that is usually telling you the routine itself needs changing.
  • When workers are uncertain. If staff are asking each other how to do something, the instructions are not clear enough, and that is a clinical governance issue rather than a training inconvenience.

What to look for in a provider

Four questions sort this out quickly.

  1. Is the nurse a registered nurse with current AHPRA registration, and is that registration one you can check yourself?
  2. Does the same nurse stay with me, or do I get whoever is rostered? Continuity is most of the value, because noticing change depends on knowing the baseline.
  3. Does the nurse train and sign off the support workers who will be in my home, or is that handled somewhere else by someone who has never met me?
  4. What is the arrangement after hours and on weekends, and who do workers phone when something looks wrong at the weekend?

The third question is the one that separates an integrated service from two services stapled together. An arrangement where the nursing provider and the support provider are different organisations can work perfectly well, but only if somebody has been explicit about who owns the care plan and who trains the workers. When that is left vague, it tends to be nobody.

It is also fair to ask how often the plan gets reviewed, and to expect a specific answer rather than as needed.

Common questions

Frequently asked

What does a community nurse do that a support worker cannot?
Assessment and clinical judgement. A nurse decides whether something has changed, what to do about it, and which tasks can safely be delegated. A support worker carries out what the nurse has set up, within the limits the nurse has written.
Is a community nurse the same as a district nurse?
The terms overlap and are often used interchangeably in Australia. District nursing usually refers to health-funded services, while community nursing in a disability context is funded through the NDIS.
How often would a community nurse visit?
It depends entirely on the clinical need. Some people see a nurse daily, others fortnightly, others only for a review every few months while support workers handle the routine in between.
Does the NDIS pay for community nursing?
Yes, where the need is disability related. Health conditions unrelated to your disability remain the responsibility of the health system, and the two can sit side by side in one person's care.
Can a community nurse train my support workers?
Yes, and for high intensity supports the NDIS Practice Standards expect a suitably qualified health practitioner to do exactly that, for each worker and each specific task.
Do I need a doctor's referral?
Not for NDIS-funded nursing. You need relevant funding in your plan and a provider who can deliver it. Your GP or specialist will usually be involved in the clinical picture regardless.
Do you take referrals for complex NDIS participants?
Yes. Abundance Healthcare takes referrals from coordinators, discharge planners and families for complex and high-intensity NDIS care. Submit an enquiry and we’ll respond, usually the same business day.
